name: Basic
desc: Foundation concepts across Claude API, Claude Code and MCP — plus the 12 official sample questions published in the CCAR-F Exam Guide

questions.q: Your app needs to process 10,000 support tickets overnight for classification. Live responses aren't needed and cost efficiency matters most. What should you use?
options: Streaming Messages API fanned out across many concurrent worker connections
Message Batches API, which processes large request sets asynchronously at reduced cost
Extended thinking with a high budget_tokens value on each classification request
One synchronous request that packs all tickets into a single prompt-cached context
questions.explain: The Message Batches API is purpose-built for large asynchronous workloads and costs less per token than live calls. High-concurrency streaming is the tempting near-miss: it does raise throughput but bills at standard rates and adds rate-limit pressure, so it misses the cost-efficiency requirement.

questions.q: You need Claude to always return valid JSON matching a specific schema. Which combination is most reliable?
options: A stop_sequences list of closing braces so output is truncated to valid JSON only
A schema in the system prompt with temperature raised so Claude explores valid variants
Extended thinking enabled so Claude self-checks the JSON shape before emitting it
A schema in the system prompt plus assistant prefill, with a validate-and-retry loop
questions.explain: Reliability comes from combining a clear schema, prefilling the assistant turn to anchor the format, and programmatically retrying on validation failure. The extended-thinking option is the strong near-miss: internal reasoning can improve quality but provides no guarantee of schema conformance, so you still need external validation.

questions.q: Why is the Messages API described as 'stateless'?
options: Conversation state is retained only for the lifetime of a single streaming connection
Every request must carry the full conversation history; no turns are stored server-side
State is kept server-side but expires once the prompt cache TTL elapses for that prefix
Only the system prompt persists between calls; user and assistant turns must be resent
questions.explain: Stateless means the API stores nothing between calls, so the client resends the entire message list each time. 'Retained for the lifetime of a streaming connection' is the tempting near-miss: streaming only affects how one response is delivered, and no turn history survives even within that connection.

questions.q: A tool_use block comes back from Claude. What's the correct next step?
options: Your application executes the tool and returns the output as a tool_result content block
Your application returns the output as a new user text message describing what happened
The API executes the tool server-side and you simply poll for the follow-up assistant turn
You resend the same request with tool_choice set to none so Claude answers from context
questions.explain: In the client-side tool loop your code runs the tool and sends back a tool_result block referencing the matching tool_use id. Returning the output as plain user text is the near-miss: Claude may cope, but the block linkage is lost and the API rejects an unanswered tool_use.

questions.q: Your team keeps manually repeating the same 5-step debugging workflow in Claude Code. What's the best fix?
options: Register a pre-tool-use hook that injects the debugging steps whenever Bash is called
Store the workflow in project CLAUDE.md so it loads into context every single session
Define it as a subagent so each debugging step runs in its own isolated context window
Create a custom slash command that encodes the whole workflow as one invocation
questions.explain: A custom slash command is the built-in way to turn a repeated multi-step procedure into one reusable, parameterized invocation. Putting it in CLAUDE.md is the tempting near-miss: it does share the steps with the team, but it burns context every session and still has to be triggered manually.

questions.q: A project-level CLAUDE.md and a user-level CLAUDE.md give conflicting instructions. Which takes precedence?
options: The more specific, local configuration wins, so project-level overrides user-level
User-level wins, since personal preferences are loaded last and override project files
The files are concatenated and Claude asks you which conflicting instruction to follow
Whichever file is larger is treated as authoritative for the overlapping instructions
questions.explain: Memory files cascade from broad to specific, and the closest scope to the work (project, then directory) takes precedence on conflicts. 'User-level loaded last' is the near-miss: load order is real, but it runs the other way, with narrower project context taking priority.

questions.q: You're asking Claude Code to refactor a large, ambiguous, cross-file system. What should happen first?
options: Claude should make the edits and rely on a stop hook to revert anything that breaks
Claude should read the whole repo into context first, then edit as understanding forms
Claude should use plan mode to propose an approach for review before editing any file
Claude should split the refactor across separate subagents that each pick a strategy
questions.explain: For large, ambiguous, cross-file work, plan mode surfaces the intended approach so you can correct it before any write happens. Reading the repo first is the tempting near-miss: context gathering is useful but it is not a review gate, and edits can still begin from a wrong plan.

questions.q: What's the primary use of hooks in Claude Code?
options: Running validation, logging, or blocking of risky actions before or after a step
Injecting extra reference files into context at the moment a tool result is returned
Retrying a failed tool call automatically with adjusted parameters until it succeeds
Routing certain prompts to a cheaper model to reduce token spend on simple requests
questions.explain: Hooks are shell commands wired to lifecycle events, letting you validate, log, or block an action deterministically. 'Injecting extra reference files' is the near-miss: some hooks can add context, but that is a side effect, not the primary purpose of enforcement and observability.

questions.q: An MCP server exposes 40 near-identical tools, and Claude keeps picking the wrong one. What's the real problem and fix?
options: Reasoning overload from many near-identical tools; consolidate and scope them tightly
Ambiguous parameter schemas; add enum constraints to every argument on all 40 tools
Tool descriptions truncated by the client; shorten each name so all 40 fit in context
Missing tool_choice configuration; force a specific tool on every turn to remove doubt
questions.explain: Large sets of overlapping tools make selection ambiguous, so the fix is consolidating and narrowing tool surface area. Tightening parameter schemas is the tempting near-miss: better schemas help argument accuracy but do nothing to disambiguate which of 40 similar tools to call.

questions.q: When should you choose SSE/HTTP transport over stdio for an MCP server?
options: When the server is written in a language that cannot read and write standard streams
When the server is local but needs to stream partial tool results back incrementally
When the server must handle several concurrent requests from one local desktop client
When the server must be reachable remotely and serve multiple users with authentication
questions.explain: stdio fits local single-user processes; HTTP/SSE exists for remote servers that need network reachability, multi-user access, and auth. Streaming partial results is the near-miss: it sounds transport-specific, but stdio already carries incremental messages, so streaming is not the deciding factor.

questions.q: You're designing an MCP tool that can permanently delete production records. What must the design include?
options: An explicit confirmation step that must be satisfied before the irreversible call runs
A dry_run parameter defaulting to true, with the description warning about data loss
Rate limiting on the endpoint so no more than a few records can be removed per minute
A read-only companion tool listing affected records that Claude is instructed to call first
questions.explain: Destructive, irreversible operations need a real confirmation gate enforced at the tool boundary, not left to model judgment. The dry_run default is the strongest near-miss: it reduces accidents but the model can still set dry_run to false in the same turn, so nothing actually blocks the deletion.

questions.q: What's the fundamental relationship between an MCP client and server?
options: The server hosts the model and the client supplies only the transport and the user prompt
The client registers its available tools with the server, which then decides when to invoke them
Both sides publish capabilities symmetrically and either may expose tools to the other
The server exposes tools and resources; the client, such as Claude, discovers and calls them
questions.explain: MCP servers publish capabilities (tools, resources, prompts) and MCP clients like Claude connect, discover, and invoke them. The symmetric-capabilities option is the near-miss: clients do expose some features such as sampling, but tools and resources flow from server to client, not both ways.

questions.q: You can describe exactly what 'done' looks like (all tests pass, zero type errors) better than the steps to get there. Which approach fits best?
options: Use /compact between attempts so the running summary preserves only the failing test names
Use plan mode so the proposed steps are reviewed before any of the refactoring begins
Re-run the same prompt on a fixed interval until the test suite eventually comes back green
Use /goal to set a completion condition so Claude iterates until an evaluator confirms it
questions.explain: When the finish line is easier to specify than the path, a goal with a completion condition lets Claude keep working until a fast evaluator verifies it. Plan mode is the tempting near-miss: it structures the approach up front but has no mechanism for checking whether 'done' was ever reached.

questions.q: Your team has a hard rule: never push to main. Where should it live so Claude cannot skip it?
options: Implement it as a pre-tool-use hook that inspects the command and blocks the push outright
Declare it in your local user-scoped CLAUDE.md so it applies across all of your repositories
Declare it in project CLAUDE.md as an IMPORTANT rule so every session loads the constraint
Document it in a skill's reference.md that Claude reads whenever git operations come up
questions.explain: Only a pre-tool-use hook enforces the rule in code, inspecting the command and denying it deterministically. Project CLAUDE.md marked IMPORTANT is the tempting near-miss: it strongly influences behavior but remains guidance a model can overlook under pressure.

questions.q: You've typed the same multi-step procedure more than once, and it includes long reference material and a helper script. How should you package it?
options: Register it as an organization-level managed policy so the procedure is applied automatically
Package it as a skill with every step and the full reference material written inline in skill.md
Paste the whole procedure plus reference material into project CLAUDE.md for the team to share
Package it as a skill with a lean skill.md, pushing depth into reference.md and helper scripts
questions.explain: Skills use progressive disclosure: a short skill.md that Claude always sees, with bulky reference files and scripts loaded only when needed. Writing everything inline in skill.md is the near-miss: it is still a skill, but it defeats progressive disclosure and consumes context on every invocation.

questions.q: You ask Claude in auto mode to refactor authentication and it writes broken authentication. What happens, and what should you add?
options: The safety classifier allows it since broken code is not dangerous; add a stop hook running tests
The safety classifier flags the edit because authentication code is treated as security sensitive
Plan mode would have prevented it by validating the refactor's correctness before any writes
Bypass permissions would have surfaced it by prompting on each individual file modification
questions.explain: Auto mode's classifier screens actions for danger, not for correctness, so safe-but-broken code passes through; a stop hook that runs your tests catches it. The plan-mode option is the tempting near-miss: review of the approach is valuable but it cannot verify the code that gets written.

questions.q: You want a dependency audit to run every morning at 9am with no machine of yours staying on and no workflow file to maintain. Which fits?
options: A routine running on Anthropic-hosted infrastructure, started by a cron-style schedule trigger
A headless claude -p invocation wired to a cron entry on one of your own always-on machines
The Agent SDK embedded in a small service you deploy so the audit runs on your own schedule
A GitHub Actions workflow on a schedule trigger, calling Claude Code from the action runner
questions.explain: A hosted routine with a cron trigger satisfies all three constraints: nothing of yours stays powered on and there is no workflow file to maintain. The GitHub Actions option is the strongest near-miss: the runner is not your machine, but you still author and maintain a workflow file.

questions.q: Your team wants Claude to review every PR with inline comments, nothing to build or host, and no approve/block needed. Which fits?
options: Managed code review via the Claude GitHub app, which posts inline comments once installed
The Claude Code GitHub action with a workflow file that comments on each pull request event
A headless claude -p run behind a webhook receiver your team deploys and keeps available
The /code-review command run locally by each reviewer before they approve the pull request
questions.explain: The managed GitHub app is installed rather than built, and it posts inline review comments automatically without gating merges. The GitHub action is the tempting near-miss: it produces the same comments but requires you to author and maintain a workflow file.

questions.q: A job ran unattended in CI and reports success. What's the most reliable first move before shipping?
options: Read Claude's end-of-run summary and confirm it lists the same files the ticket mentioned
Start from the diff itself and confirm from test output that the suite genuinely passed
Re-run the identical prompt in a fresh session and compare the two summaries for agreement
Check that the run exited with status zero and that no tool calls were denied by permissions
questions.explain: A self-reported success is a claim, so verification means inspecting the actual diff and the real test output. Checking the exit status is the tempting near-miss: it is objective evidence, but a run can exit cleanly while tests were skipped, filtered, or never invoked.

questions.q: A community plugin gives you a skill you want. What should you do before enabling it?
options: Confirm it comes from a marketplace that runs automated review before publishing submissions
Inspect every hook, agent, and MCP server it adds, since plugin code runs with your privileges
Rely on plugin namespacing to keep its commands and agents from colliding with your own
Enable it in a throwaway project first and rely on permission prompts to catch anything risky
questions.explain: A plugin can contribute hooks, agents, and MCP servers that execute with your own privileges and fire automatically, so you review its contents before enabling. The sandboxed-trial option is the tempting near-miss: isolation helps, but hooks run as shell commands outside the permission prompts you would be watching for.

questions.q: What's the simplest way to share a skill with your whole team, requiring zero extra installation?
options: Package it as a plugin and publish it to an internal marketplace teammates must add first
Distribute it through enterprise managed settings so IT pushes it to every developer machine
Commit it under .claude/skills in the repo so everyone who clones the project gets it
Place it in each teammate's ~/.claude/skills directory as part of onboarding setup
questions.explain: Skills committed to .claude/skills in the repo travel with the clone, so no installation step is needed. The plugin-marketplace option is tempting because marketplaces do distribute skills, but each teammate still has to add the marketplace and install the plugin.

questions.q: Two skills share a name: one at enterprise (managed settings) level, one at project level. Which wins?
options: Project-level wins, since the more specific scope always overrides broader configuration
Both load side by side and Claude picks whichever description matches the request better
Enterprise managed settings win, taking highest priority so admins can enforce standards
The user-level ~/.claude copy is promoted to break the tie between the two conflicting scopes
questions.explain: Managed (enterprise) settings sit at the top of the precedence chain precisely so administrators can enforce mandatory standards. 'Project-level wins because it is more specific' is the tempting near-miss: specificity governs many config systems, but Claude Code deliberately puts managed settings above project scope.

questions.q: You delegate a task to a sub-agent. Does it automatically have access to your main conversation's skills?
options: Sub-agents start fresh; only custom sub-agents can use skills, and only when listed in their config
Sub-agents inherit the parent conversation's loaded skills along with its accumulated context
Built-in sub-agents such as Explore receive skills, while custom sub-agents must request them
Skills become available to a sub-agent only once it has read the project's CLAUDE.md file
questions.explain: Sub-agents begin with fresh context, and skills are available only to custom sub-agents that explicitly list them. The inheritance option is the strong near-miss: sub-agents do receive their task prompt from the parent, but not its loaded skills or context.

questions.q: What does it mean that MCP is 'transport agnostic'?
options: Servers advertise a transport during initialize, and clients must implement all of them to connect
The protocol negotiates a transport at runtime, upgrading a stdio session to HTTP when remote
Message payloads are transport-neutral binary frames rather than the JSON-RPC used elsewhere
Client and server may talk over different transports: stdio locally, or HTTP for remote servers
questions.explain: Transport agnostic means the JSON-RPC message layer is independent of the channel carrying it: stdio for local processes, HTTP-based transports for remote ones. The runtime-upgrade option sounds plausible but no transport negotiation or stdio-to-HTTP upgrade exists; the transport is chosen when the connection is configured.

questions.q: In the MCP tool-calling flow, what are the two core message-type pairs exchanged?
options: InitializeRequest/Result to handshake, and CallToolRequest/Result to execute a chosen tool
ListToolsRequest/Result to discover tools, and CallToolRequest/Result to execute one
ListToolsRequest/Result to discover tools, and ToolResultNotification to stream back output
ListPromptsRequest/Result to enumerate capabilities, and GetPromptRequest/Result to run them
questions.explain: Tool use runs on two request/result pairs: ListTools to discover what exists, then CallTool to invoke one. The initialize pairing is the near-miss: initialize really is exchanged, but it is the connection handshake, not part of the tool-calling flow itself.

questions.q: Using the Python MCP SDK's decorator approach, how does the SDK know a tool's arguments and descriptions?
options: Type hints on the parameters plus field descriptions, from which the SDK generates the schema
A JSON schema you supply in the decorator's schema argument, which the SDK forwards unchanged
Runtime introspection of the first few calls, from which the SDK infers argument types over time
The function's docstring only, which the SDK parses into both parameter names and their types
questions.explain: The decorator reads Python type annotations and field descriptions and generates the JSON schema for you. The docstring-only answer is the tempting near-miss: the docstring does supply the tool description, but parameter types come from the annotations, not from parsing prose.

questions.q: What is the MCP Inspector primarily used for?
options: A local browser-based tool for connecting to a server and testing its tools, resources, prompts
A CLI validator that checks a server's schemas against the MCP spec and reports violations
A proxy that records production client-server traffic so failed tool calls can be replayed later
A scaffolding utility that reads your server code and generates a matching test client harness
questions.explain: The Inspector is a development-time UI you point at a local server to exercise its tools, resources, and prompts interactively. The schema-validator option is plausible because the Inspector does surface schema problems, but it is an interactive testing client, not a spec-conformance linter.

questions.q: On the client side, what two core functions does your MCP client class typically implement for tools?
options: get_capabilities() to enumerate server features, and send_request() to dispatch any raw message
connect() to open the session, and call_tool() to invoke a tool once the session is ready
list_tools() to discover tools, and read_resource() to fetch each tool's output payload
list_tools() to discover available tools, and call_tool() to invoke one with arguments
questions.explain: A client wrapper normally exposes list_tools() for discovery and call_tool() for execution. The connect()/call_tool() pairing tempts because a session must indeed be established first, but connection setup is lifecycle plumbing rather than one of the two tool operations.

questions.q: What's the key difference between a 'direct' and a 'templated' resource in MCP?
options: Direct resources are read once and cached, while templated resources are re-fetched on every read
Direct resources are listed by resources/list, while templated ones are only returned by tools/call
Direct resources expose a static URI; templated resources embed parameters parsed into your function
Direct resources return a single content block; templated resources always return a list of blocks
questions.explain: A direct resource has a fixed, parameter-free URI; a templated resource carries URI parameters that are parsed and handed to your handler. The listing-based option is the near-miss: templates really do appear separately from concrete resources in listing, but via resources/templates/list, and they are still read through resources/read.

questions.q: Why prefer a resource over a tool call to get document content into a Claude conversation?
options: Resource reads bypass the model's context window entirely, so document size never costs tokens
The app can inject the content into context up front, avoiding a separate model-initiated fetch
Resources are fetched during initialize, so the content is present before the first user message
Resource content is exempt from tool-use permission prompts, so the read completes without approval
questions.explain: Resources are application-controlled, so your app can pull the document and place it in context directly instead of waiting for Claude to decide to call a tool. The 'never costs tokens' option is tempting but wrong: injected resource content still occupies the context window.

questions.q: Your MCP client reads a resource with MIME type 'application/json'. What should it do with the text?
options: Re-request the resource with a blob content type so the JSON arrives already decoded by the SDK
Store the text verbatim and let the model parse the JSON when it reasons over the content
Validate the text against the resource's declared schema and reject the read if it does not match
Parse the returned text as JSON into a structured object instead of handling it as a raw string
questions.explain: The MIME type tells the client how to interpret the payload, so application/json text should be parsed into a structured object. Leaving it verbatim for the model is the plausible near-miss: it may still work, but it discards the very hint the MIME type exists to provide.

questions.q: Why define a custom prompt (like a /format command) instead of letting users type free-form instructions?
options: A named prompt is cached by the server, so repeated invocations skip re-processing the instructions
Server-defined prompts are validated against the tool schemas, so malformed instructions are caught
A pre-built, tested template encodes expertise and handles edge cases consistently for every user
Prompt templates run with elevated permissions, letting them call tools a user request cannot reach
questions.explain: A prompt authored and tested once bakes in expertise and edge-case handling that ad-hoc user phrasing will not reproduce reliably. The caching option is the tempting distractor: prompt caching is a real API feature, but MCP prompts are not automatically cached by the server on invocation.

questions.q: Your MCP client calls get_prompt on your server with arguments like {"doc_id": "plan.md"} — what happens to that value?
options: The value is resolved as a resource URI first, and the fetched content replaces the placeholder
The value is validated against the prompt's argument list and then attached as message metadata
The value is interpolated into the template, filling the placeholder the prompt declares
The value is forwarded to the matching tool, whose result becomes the returned prompt message
questions.explain: Arguments reach the server handler as parameters and are substituted into the message template it returns. The resource-resolution option is the near-miss: a document id looks like something to fetch, but the server only substitutes the string unless its own code chooses to read a resource.

questions.q: MCP has three primitives: tools, resources, prompts. Which part of the stack controls each?
options: All three are server-controlled, with the client only rendering whatever the server advertises
Tools are model-controlled, prompts are application-controlled, resources are user-controlled
Tools and prompts are both model-controlled, while resources remain under application control
Tools are model-controlled, resources are application-controlled, prompts are user-controlled
questions.explain: The standard mental model: Claude decides on tools, the host application decides on resources, and the user explicitly triggers prompts. Swapping prompts and resources is the tempting near-miss, but prompts are the user-facing primitive surfaced as slash commands or buttons.

questions.q: You're deciding how to implement a feature: users click a button to trigger a 'summarize document' workflow. Which MCP primitive?
options: Resources, because the workflow's document data must be read into context before summarizing
Tools, because summarization is a new capability the model needs exposed to it explicitly
Prompts, because the user explicitly triggers when the summarize workflow should start
Sampling, because the server needs the host to run a completion on the user's behalf
questions.explain: A button the user clicks to launch a workflow is user-initiated, which is exactly what prompts model. Tools is the strongest distractor since summarization sounds like a capability, but tools are invoked by the model's own choice rather than by a direct user action.

questions.q: You need Claude Code in a CI pipeline producing identical, reproducible results on every machine, with no teammate's local hook or project MCP server interfering. Which flag?
options: --dangerously-skip-permissions, which runs non-interactively without any approval prompts
--strict-mcp-config, which limits MCP servers to those named on the command line for the run
--bare, which skips discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, memory, and CLAUDE.md
--settings with an empty JSON object, which replaces every discovered configuration layer
questions.explain: --bare skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, memory, and CLAUDE.md, so a run is identical on any machine (note that it also skips OAuth, so use ANTHROPIC_API_KEY). --strict-mcp-config is the near-miss: it really does control MCP discovery, but it leaves hooks, skills, and CLAUDE.md in play.

questions.q: SCENARIO — Customer Support Resolution Agent (Claude + MCP tools). Production data shows that in 12% of cases, your Claude agent skips get_customer entirely and calls lookup_order using only the customer's stated name, occasionally leading to misidentified accounts and incorrect refunds. What change would most effectively address this reliability issue?
options: Block lookup_order and process_refund programmatically until get_customer returns a verified ID
State in the system prompt that get_customer verification is mandatory before any order operation
Add few-shot examples where the agent calls get_customer first even when an order number is given
Route each request through a classifier that enables only the tools that request type should use
questions.explain: Critical business ordering needs deterministic enforcement in code, not probabilistic model compliance. The few-shot option is the tempting near-miss: examples do measurably improve sequencing, but they cannot guarantee it in the 12% tail where money is at stake.

questions.q: SCENARIO — Customer Support Resolution Agent. Production logs show Claude frequently calls get_customer when users ask about orders (e.g., 'check my order #12345'), instead of calling lookup_order. Both tools have minimal descriptions ('Retrieves customer information' / 'Retrieves order details') and accept similar identifier formats. What's the most effective first step to improve tool selection reliability?
options: Parse each user message for order-number patterns and pre-select the tool before the turn runs
Add five to eight few-shot exchanges to the system prompt showing correct selection between them
Merge both into one lookup_entity tool that inspects the identifier and picks the backend itself
Expand each description with input formats, sample queries, edge cases, and when-not-to-use bounds
questions.explain: Descriptions are the model's primary signal for choosing between tools, so enriching the two thin descriptions attacks the root cause cheaply. Few-shot examples are the strong near-miss: they help, but they patch symptoms with extra tokens while the ambiguous descriptions remain.

questions.q: SCENARIO — Customer Support Resolution Agent. Your Claude-powered agent achieves 55% first-contact resolution, well below the 80% target. Logs show it escalates straightforward cases (standard damage replacements with photo evidence) while attempting to autonomously handle complex situations requiring policy exceptions. What's the most effective way to improve escalation calibration?
options: Have the agent emit a 1-10 confidence score each turn and hand off anything below a threshold
Put explicit escalation criteria in the system prompt with examples of escalate versus resolve
Train a classifier on historical tickets to predict up front which requests will need escalation
Run sentiment analysis on the conversation and escalate automatically on strongly negative tone
questions.explain: The failure is an undefined decision boundary, which explicit criteria plus contrasting examples fix directly. Self-reported confidence is the tempting near-miss: it looks like a calibration control, but the agent is already overconfident on exactly the hard cases it should escalate.

questions.q: You want to create a custom /review slash command that runs your team's standard code review checklist, available to every developer when they clone or pull the repository. Where should you create this command file?
options: Define the checklist as a section inside the CLAUDE.md file at the root of the project repo
Create it in each developer's ~/.claude/commands/ directory so the command is always available
Create it in the project repository's .claude/commands/ directory so it ships with every clone
Register it in .claude/settings.json under a commands array pointing at the checklist file
questions.explain: Project-scoped slash commands live in .claude/commands/ in the repo, so they are version-controlled and appear for everyone who clones or pulls. The ~/.claude/commands/ option is the near-miss: that path does define working commands, but only for that one developer's machine.

questions.q: You've been assigned to restructure the team's monolithic application into microservices, involving changes across dozens of files and decisions about service boundaries and module dependencies. Which approach should you take?
options: Enter plan mode first to map dependencies and design the service boundaries before editing any files
Execute directly in small increments and let the emerging import graph reveal the service boundaries for you
Execute directly, but front-load one very detailed prompt that fixes each service's structure in advance
Execute directly and escalate into plan mode only once cross-module coupling starts causing broken builds
questions.explain: Plan mode exists for exactly this shape of work: many files, several viable designs, and architectural decisions worth exploring before committing. The tempting near-miss is letting the import graph reveal boundaries incrementally — it reads like discovery-driven design but it commits you to edits before the dependency picture exists, guaranteeing rework.

questions.q: Your codebase has distinct areas with different conventions (React hooks, async/await API handlers, repository-pattern DB models). Test files are spread throughout alongside the code they test (e.g., Button.test.tsx next to Button.tsx), and you want all tests to follow the same conventions regardless of location. Most maintainable way to ensure Claude auto-applies correct conventions?
options: Drop a scoped CLAUDE.md into each area's subdirectory so its conventions load whenever files there are touched
Add rule files under .claude/rules/ whose frontmatter globs apply each convention by file path automatically
Define one skill per code type under .claude/skills/, keeping each area's conventions inside its SKILL.md
Keep every convention in the root CLAUDE.md under per-area headings and let Claude match code to heading
questions.explain: Rule files with glob frontmatter (e.g. **/*.test.tsx) attach conventions to path patterns, so they fire wherever a matching file lives. The strong near-miss is per-directory CLAUDE.md files: that is a real mechanism, but it is directory-bound, so tests scattered next to their sources would each need their own copy.

questions.q: Running the system on 'impact of AI on creative industries,' each subagent completes successfully, but final reports cover only visual arts, missing music, writing, and film. The coordinator's logs show it decomposed the topic into 'AI in digital art creation,' 'AI in graphic design,' and 'AI in photography.' Most likely root cause?
options: The synthesis agent has no instruction to audit incoming findings for topic-coverage gaps before writing
The coordinator decomposed the topic too narrowly, so the subagent assignments never spanned all creative domains
The search agent's query templates are too literal, so they retrieve only the visual-arts phrasing of the topic
The document analysis agent's relevance threshold is discarding music, writing, and film sources as off-topic
questions.explain: The coordinator's own logs show all three subtasks were visual-arts framings, so the omission was baked into decomposition and the subagents completed exactly what they were given. The tempting near-miss blames the synthesis agent for not auditing coverage — a gap check might surface the symptom, but the missing domains were never researched, so synthesis has nothing to recover.

questions.q: The web search subagent times out while researching a complex topic. You need to design how this failure flows back to the coordinator. Which error propagation approach best enables intelligent recovery?
options: Absorb the timeout in the subagent and hand back an empty result set flagged as a successful completion
Retry inside the subagent with exponential backoff, returning a generic 'search unavailable' once retries end
Return structured error context: failure type, the attempted query, any partial results, and alternatives
Let the timeout bubble to a top-level handler that halts the research workflow and reports the stage reached
questions.explain: Structured context is what lets the coordinator choose intelligently between narrowing the query, substituting a source, or proceeding on partial results. The tempting near-miss is in-subagent retry with backoff: retrying is reasonable, but collapsing the outcome to a generic status destroys the query and partial results the coordinator needs to recover.

questions.q: SCENARIO — Multi-Agent Research System built on the Claude Agent SDK. The synthesis subagent frequently needs to verify claims while combining findings. Currently it returns control to the coordinator, which invokes web search, then re-invokes synthesis — adding 2-3 round trips and 40% latency. 85% of verifications are simple fact-checks (dates, names, statistics); 15% need deeper investigation. Most effective approach?
options: Have the search agent cache extra surrounding context per source, anticipating what synthesis will later ask
Grant the synthesis agent the full web search toolset so it can resolve any verification without a round trip
Have synthesis collect every verification need and hand them back to the coordinator as one batch at the end
Give synthesis a scoped verify_fact tool for simple lookups and keep deep checks routed via the coordinator
questions.explain: A scoped verify_fact tool removes the round trips for the 85% simple case while leaving genuine investigation with the specialist agent — least privilege plus latency win. The tempting near-miss is handing synthesis the whole search toolset: it does kill the round trips, but it over-provisions and dissolves the separation of concerns that keeps the 15% deep cases reliable.

questions.q: Your pipeline script runs claude "Analyze this pull request for security issues" but the job hangs indefinitely; logs indicate Claude Code is waiting for interactive input. Correct approach to run Claude Code in an automated pipeline?
options: Export CLAUDE_CODE_NONINTERACTIVE=1 in the job environment so the CLI skips its interactive startup path
Redirect stdin from /dev/null so the session sees EOF immediately and falls through to prompt processing
Pass the -p/--print flag so the prompt is processed non-interactively and output goes to stdout
Pass --output-format json, which implies non-interactive execution because streamed UI output is disabled
questions.explain: -p (--print) is the documented non-interactive mode: it runs the prompt, prints the result, and exits, which is what CI needs. The tempting near-miss is redirecting stdin from /dev/null — a real Unix trick that may stop the hang, but it does not select print mode, so you are relying on side effects rather than the supported flag; the env var shown is not a real setting and --output-format alone does not imply -p.

questions.q: Your team wants to reduce API costs. Real-time Claude calls power two workflows: (1) a blocking pre-merge check developers wait on before merging, and (2) an overnight technical-debt report for next-morning review. Your manager proposes switching both to the Message Batches API for 50% savings. How should you evaluate this?
options: Move both to the Batches API and poll batch status, since most batches complete well inside a few minutes
Move only the overnight technical-debt report to the Batches API and keep the pre-merge check on real time
Move both to the Batches API but fall back to real-time calls whenever a batch exceeds a latency threshold
Keep both on real-time calls, because batch responses return unordered and cannot be matched to requests
questions.explain: The Batches API trades roughly 50% cost for asynchronous processing with up to a 24-hour window, which fits an overnight report and not a check developers block on. The tempting near-miss is batching both and polling because batches 'usually' finish fast: typical speed is not a guarantee, so a blocking pre-merge gate would intermittently stall; the ordering claim is also wrong since custom_id matches results back to requests.

questions.q: SCENARIO — Claude Code for Continuous Integration. A pull request modifies 14 files across the stock tracking module. Your single-pass Claude Code review analyzing all files together produces inconsistent results: detailed feedback for some, superficial for others, obvious bugs missed, and contradictory feedback (flagging a pattern in one file while approving identical code elsewhere in the same PR). How should you restructure?
options: Run the full pull request through three independent passes and report only findings that recur in two
Gate the pipeline so developers must break large pull requests into 3-4 file chunks before review runs
Move to a larger-context model so all 14 files fit comfortably and each receives equal analytical depth
Split it up: review each file individually, then run one integration pass over cross-file data flow
questions.explain: Per-file passes give each file consistent depth and a dedicated integration pass recovers the cross-file reasoning, addressing attention dilution directly. The tempting near-miss is a bigger context window: the 14 files likely already fit, and capacity does not fix how attention is distributed across them.

questions.q: Your user settings allow Bash(curl *), the project settings.json denies it, and IT has deployed a managed policy that also denies it. You add an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json. What is the effective result?
options: curl is allowed — an explicit allow rule always takes priority over a deny rule at any settings scope
curl is allowed — local settings sit above project settings, so the local allow rule resolves the conflict
curl stays denied — managed policy sits above every other scope and cannot be loosened from below
Claude Code refuses to start the session and reports a permission conflict across the settings scopes
questions.explain: Precedence runs managed above CLI flags, local, project, then user, so an enterprise managed deny is final regardless of what lower scopes allow. The tempting near-miss is 'local beats project' — true on its own, but irrelevant here because the managed deny still sits above the local allow.

questions.q: In Claude Code settings.json, how do permission rules behave differently from ordinary settings keys when multiple scopes define them?
options: Permission rules resolve like every other key: the highest-precedence scope's arrays replace the lower ones
The allow, ask, and deny arrays from all scopes merge into one effective policy instead of being replaced
Only the managed and project scopes contribute rules; local and user permission arrays are read but ignored
Arrays merge, but a later scope's allow entry removes any matching deny entry contributed by an earlier scope
questions.explain: Ordinary settings keys take the winning scope's value, whereas permission arrays are unioned across scopes into a single policy evaluated before each tool call — which is why a deny anywhere in the chain still bites. The tempting near-miss says arrays merge but allows cancel denies; merging is right, cancellation is not, since deny takes priority within the merged policy.

questions.q: A teammate writes a PreToolUse hook to block edits to production config. It detects the violation and exits with code 1, printing the reason to stderr. The edit still goes through. Why?
options: The matcher must name the tool explicitly, as a wildcard PreToolUse matcher runs in advisory mode only
Blocking requires the JSON decision object on stdout; a bare non-zero exit code is only logged as a warning
The reason must go to stdout, since Claude Code discards a PreToolUse hook's stderr stream entirely
Exit 1 is treated as a non-blocking error — only exit 2 blocks and returns stderr to Claude as the reason
questions.explain: For PreToolUse, exit 0 allows, exit 2 blocks and feeds stderr back to Claude as the reason, and any other non-zero code is a non-blocking error — so the conventional exit 1 blocks nothing. The tempting near-miss is 'you must emit JSON on stdout': structured JSON output is a real alternative way to decide, but it is not required, and exit 2 alone would have worked.

questions.q: A session is running with bypassPermissions. A PreToolUse hook returns permissionDecision 'deny' for a dangerous command. What happens, and what's the inverse case?
options: It is blocked, and the inverse holds too — a hook returning allow overrides a settings deny symmetrically
It is blocked: PreToolUse hooks evaluate ahead of the permission mode, and a hook allow cannot undo a deny rule
It runs, because bypassPermissions short-circuits the permission pipeline before any PreToolUse hook fires
It runs, because hook decisions are advisory once the session starts in bypassPermissions or skip mode
questions.explain: PreToolUse hooks run before permission-mode evaluation, so a hook deny stops the command even under bypassPermissions, yet hooks can only tighten policy — an allow will not override a settings-level deny. The tempting near-miss agrees on the block but claims symmetry; that inverse does not hold.

questions.q: You want to guarantee a formatter runs after every file edit, and separately to guarantee a dangerous command never executes. Which hook events, and what's the key limitation to understand?
options: PreToolUse blocks the dangerous command before it runs; PostToolUse formats after an edit but cannot undo it
PostToolUse handles both, since it inspects each completed call and can revert one that violated a policy
PreToolUse handles both: it fires before the tool and again after it returns, so it can format the written file
UserPromptSubmit handles both by rewriting the request before any tool call is planned or executed
questions.explain: PreToolUse is the checkpoint that can stop a call before execution, while PostToolUse fires after success and is the right place to format, lint, or test — but it cannot roll the call back, so anything that must never happen belongs in PreToolUse. The tempting near-miss has PostToolUse reverting violations; it can report and even feed back to Claude, but the tool call has already taken effect.

questions.q: The same MCP server name is defined at local, project, and user scope with different configs. Which one loads?
options: Project scope wins — the committed .mcp.json entry is authoritative so every teammate resolves it identically
Local scope wins — precedence runs local, then project, then user, and it shadows the others silently
User scope wins — it is the global definition and therefore sits at the top of the MCP resolution chain
The configs are merged field by field, with narrower scopes overriding only the keys they actually define
questions.explain: MCP scope precedence is local over project over user, and a local definition shadows a same-named server at a wider scope without any warning; claude mcp get <name> shows which one resolved. The tempting near-miss is field-by-field merging — plausible given how other settings behave, but same-named servers are shadowed wholesale, not blended.

questions.q: You run `claude mcp add sentry --transport http https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp` and expect teammates to get it on their next pull, but nothing appears in the repo. What went wrong?
options: HTTP transport entries are stored in the user config only; a committable .mcp.json accepts stdio servers
Without --scope the server lands at user scope in ~/.claude.json, which is shared but still not committable
Without --scope the server lands at local scope in ~/.claude.json; use --scope project to write .mcp.json
The command has to be run from the repository root, otherwise the generated .mcp.json goes to your home
questions.explain: claude mcp add defaults to local scope, stored in ~/.claude.json keyed by project path and private to you, so -s project is what writes a shareable .mcp.json at the repo root. The tempting near-miss names user scope instead: same file, wrong default, and it would misleadingly suggest the entry applies across all your projects.

questions.q: A developer clones a repo containing .mcp.json, runs claude, and reports the project's MCP servers show as unavailable. Nothing is misconfigured. What's happening?
options: Cloned .mcp.json entries load read-only until each server is re-registered locally with claude mcp add
Project servers from a cloned .mcp.json start unapproved by design — approve them from /mcp in a session
The file only takes effect once renamed .mcp.local.json, which is the form Claude Code actually reads
Project scope entries require a matching enabledMcpjsonServers entry in the user settings before loading
questions.explain: Servers arriving in a repo's .mcp.json sit in a pending-approval state deliberately, since code from a clone should not auto-connect; /mcp approves them and claude mcp reset-project-choices reopens the prompt. The tempting near-miss says you must re-register each server locally — that would work by accident but misses that approval, not registration, is the missing step.

questions.q: In an allowedTools list or a permission rule, how is a tool provided by an MCP server named?
options: The bare tool name, e.g. send-message, since the server namespace is resolved at connection time
Server-prefixed dot notation such as discord.send-message, matching how the server advertises the tool
Fully qualified as mcp__<server>__<tool>, for example mcp__discord__send-message in the rule or tool list
As mcp:<server>/<tool>, e.g. mcp:discord/send-message, mirroring the URI form used by MCP resources
questions.explain: Permission rules and tool lists must use the fully qualified mcp__<server>__<tool> form. The tempting near-miss is the bare tool name on the theory that the namespace resolves at connect time — it does not, and an unqualified entry silently never matches, which is a common reason a rule appears to do nothing.

questions.q: In the Agent SDK, what is the practical difference between the 'default' and 'dontAsk' permission modes?
options: dontAsk pre-approves every tool for speed, while default denies anything absent from the allow rules
In default, unmatched tools go to canUseTool; in dontAsk the callback still runs but its reply is auto-approved
In default, unmatched tools go to your canUseTool callback; in dontAsk anything not pre-approved is denied
default only applies to interactive sessions, while dontAsk is the mode headless SDK runs select by default
questions.explain: default sends tools not covered by allow rules to canUseTool for a runtime decision, while dontAsk turns every would-be prompt into a denial, so pre-approved tools run and nothing else does. The tempting near-miss keeps canUseTool firing under dontAsk with replies auto-approved; in reality the callback is bypassed entirely and the call is refused.

questions.q: An Agent SDK deployment sets allowed_tools to a short read-only list but also enables bypassPermissions for speed. A code review flags this as unsafe. Why?
options: bypassPermissions narrows to allowed_tools but skips the prompt, so any listed write tool now runs unattended
allowed_tools is not a hard boundary under bypassPermissions — unlisted tools fall through and simply run
The two options conflict, so the SDK raises a configuration error as soon as the session is initialised
bypassPermissions only covers file edits, so the read-only surface holds for every other tool category
questions.explain: bypassPermissions approves everything, so an allow list stops functioning as a boundary and unlisted tools run rather than being denied; a genuinely restricted surface needs dontAsk, deny rules, or a PreToolUse hook. The tempting near-miss claims bypass still narrows to allowed_tools and merely skips the prompt — that would make the config safe, but the list does not constrain it.

questions.q: You're defining a research subagent in the Agent SDK and want it to break its work into further parallel subtasks. What should you know?
options: Only subagents defined programmatically rather than as filesystem definitions are permitted to nest
Add the Agent/Task tool to the subagent's tool list, which is how a subagent is granted its own fan-out
Nesting works to arbitrary depth provided max_turns is raised enough to cover the child agents' turns
Subagents cannot spawn subagents, so leave Agent/Task out of their tools and keep fan-out at the orchestrator
questions.explain: Subagents cannot spawn further subagents, so granting them the Agent/Task tool is a dead end and parallel fan-out has to be organised by the orchestrator. The tempting near-miss is simply adding Agent/Task to the subagent's tools — the syntax is valid and the tool name is real, but the nesting it implies is not supported.
